Dear Kevin,

If I understand correctly, you want to bin your frequencies so that you get 5 UNIQUE frequencies per bin. If this is so, I think your second bin should go from F all the way down to, and including, P (observations 6 to 16), and you'll only get 4 rather than 5 bins. Here's my try:

Assuming your data is in a data frame called data:

x <- 5 # bin length
unique_freq <- unique(data$FREQ) # unique freq values
bins <- ceiling(length(unique_freq) / x) # number of bins
binned <- rep(1:bins, each = x)[seq_along(unique_freq)] # bin unique freqs
counts <- table(data$FREQ)[as.character(unique_freq)] # how many times each
binned <- rep(binned, counts)
data$BIN <- binned

Which gives this:

Dividing a frequency list into bands
Kevin Parent <kspa...@gmail.com>: May 18 09:09AM +0900

Need a little hand with something. I'm trying to divide a word frequency
list into frequency bands. So all the first 1000 words will be assigned a
1, the second a 2, etc. I could simply make a vector with a thousand 1s,
then a thousand 2s, etc, but this ignores the issue of ties, which becomes
an issue lower down the list. I'm defining a frequency band as x (here
x=1000) words plus all the ties of the last frequency count, so in a large
corpus, a frequency band (especially in the lower ranks) might actually
consist of a few thousand items.
 
For the sake of illustration/reproducible data, suppose we have the first
two columns of the data below. We want to divide it into bands of 5, or
more in the case of ties. The third column is what we want to generate.
 
Any suggestions?
 
WORD FREQ BAND
A 3000 1
B 2500 1
C 2300 1
D 2200 1
E 2100 1
F 2000 2
G 2000 2
H 1800 2
I 1800 2
J 1800 2

"Stefan Th. Gries" <stg...@gmail.com>: May 18 01:18AM -0700

Not sure I understand you right so let me ask a (potentially stupid)
question: Do you want the frequency bins be completely determined by
the frequency value or by the number of items that then make it into a
bin or both? From your third column, I am not sure how the switch to a
new band is defined: band 1 is everything above 2K (i.e., covers
frequencies from 2K-3K), but then band 2 only covers 1800-2000?
Kevin Parent <kspa...@gmail.com>: May 18 09:57PM +0900

Not a stupid question. It's difficult to explain.
 
I want the bins to be of x length. In the real data I'm working with, this
means each bin would include, in theory, 1000 words each. Bin #1 has the
1000 most frequent words, Bin #2 has the next 1000, etc. So
sort(table(data),decreasing=T)[1:1000] would be one way of showing the
first bin.
 
But...
 
Suppose you look carefully at the data and you see that the item at
position 1000 and the one at 1001 are actually the same frequency. I don't
want to split them up just because one is later in alphabetical order or
otherwise arbitrarily sorted. So in this case, I would want the first bin
to have 1001 items (and the next bin the next 1000, assuming no tie at the
2000th position).
 
In the sample data I gave, I want to split the data into bins containing 5
elements. The first five lines go into the first bin, and the second five
go into the second bin. No problems there. However, for the third frequency
band, the fifth (overall 15th) element has the same frequency as the sixth
(Words 'O' and 'P' both have frequencies of 1400.). Rather than splitting
them up, we put them in the same bin, so this bin has six items. Bin 4 has
a similar issue: a three-way tie at the cutoff point, so this one actually
gets seven items. (Bin 5 has three leftovers, which, given Zipf's Law, is
not realistic, but I ran out of letters.)
 
 
 
 
--

"Stefan Th. Gries" <stg...@gmail.com>: May 18 06:20AM -0700

Ok, I now understand what kind of output you want, but I am not sure
- how straightforward it is to decide automatically what frequencies
to group together - would 3001 still be in the same bin as 3000, 2500,
etc.? would 4000? would 10000?
- whether it is the best approach to bin data that we know are Zipfian
into bins with large equal numbers.
 
Esp. given the second point, I would probably just go with cut(FREQ, 5):
 
table(cut(FREQ, 5))
# (498,1e+03] (1e+03,1.5e+03] (1.5e+03,2e+03] (2e+03,2.5e+03]
(2.5e+03,3e+03]
# 8 6 7 4
1
 
But maybe I'm missing something here ... Let's see what others say
Alex Perrone <boet...@gmail.com>: May 18 10:00AM -0400

To address the original question, you can construct the frequency bands
"manually" with a while-loop with condition that the remaining (sorted)
word list is not empty, with an inner while-loop for the current bin where
you keep adding items until both of the things are true: you have collected
at least binMax items in the current bin, and the current word is not tied
with the previous word. Inside the inner while-loop, remove words from the
remaining word list as they are added to the bin. After breaking out of the
inner while-loop (inside the main while-loop), you increment the bin number.
 
 
 
I can't think of an easier way like using some fancy indexing trick in R to
break ties for you and construct the bands.
 
But I think Stefan's point is the heart of it. It reminds me of a talk he
gave way back in 2008 (maybe?) on automatically detecting an 'optimal' or
'best' way to group years for historical corpus data. It's much like the
frequency bands here. Why 1000? Might there be a data-driven way to
automatically detect bins?
